title: United ISD Earns 7th Consecutive “A” Rating From Texas Education Agency
excerpt: United ISD earned its seventh consecutive “A” in the 2026 State Accountability Ratings, one of only 30 Texas districts out of 1,202 to do so.
content:
United Independent School District has earned its seventh consecutive “A” rating in the 2026 State Accountability Ratings released by the Texas Education Agency, the district announced.

Out of 1,202 districts across Texas, United ISD is one of only 30 to earn seven “A” ratings in a row since the accountability system began, according to the district.

All four of the district’s high schools — United High School, United South High School, John B. Alexander High School and Lyndon B. Johnson High School — received “A” ratings for the 2025–2026 school year. United High School was the district’s top-ranked campus with a 96.

The district has 17 campuses rated “A,” and seven campuses moved from a “B” to an “A” from the 2024–25 school year to 2025–26, the district reported. Trautmann Middle School led the middle schools with a 92, and Kazen Elementary and San Isidro Elementary tied for the top elementary spot with a 94. Trautmann Elementary is the district’s only all-“A” campus, earning “A” marks across all four accountability domains.

“Earning a 7th consecutive ‘A’ rating from the Texas Education Agency is a historic achievement that reflects a deeply ingrained culture of excellence within the United Independent School District,” Superintendent Dr. Gerardo Cruz said.

The district served more than 39,000 students across 53 campuses during the testing period, and it notes that it is the only “A”-rated district in Texas with more than 30,000 students enrolled while serving a student population that is more than 70 percent economically disadvantaged and more than 15 percent emergent bilingual. It is also one of only 51 “A”-rated districts to earn the Postsecondary Readiness Distinction for 2025–2026.

Why it matters

Seven straight “A” ratings put Laredo’s largest school district in rare company statewide — and the district itself frames the result as proof that classroom results held up even while districts across Texas navigate funding constraints and rising costs. For Webb County families, the campus-by-campus list is the practical takeaway: 17 campuses now carry an “A,” and seven more climbed into that range this year.
